## What I did

**Settings (`scribe/config.py`)** — one frozen dataclass per rule module, with defaults that are exactly the values the module constants had, and a `Settings` holding all of them. Rules now receive settings instead of reaching for a constant:

```python
def looks_like_note(text, from_bottom, settings: NoteSettings = SETTINGS) -> bool:
    return from_bottom <= settings.foot_zone and bool(NOTE_LINE.match(text))
```

The default argument keeps every existing call site working, which is why the 54 original tests needed no edits. The reasoning comments stayed next to the rules they explain; `config.py` carries only the short "what it costs when it's wrong" version.

**Config file** — `scribe.toml`, found by walking up from the document, with `--config` to override. Top-level tables are defaults; `[document."NAME"]` tables override per document, `NAME` being a name or glob. `tomllib` is stdlib on 3.11+, so no new dependency. A misspelled key is an error naming it (`unknown setting 'repeat_shore'. Known settings: ...`) rather than a line that quietly does nothing, and per-document sections are validated at load, so a typo in a section nobody exercises still fails on the first run. The committed `scribe.toml` has every setting commented out at its default, so it changes nothing and doubles as the reference.

**The report** — `<name>.report.md` beside the Markdown, listing the lossy decisions: lines dropped as furniture (with repeat counts), words rejoined across line breaks, footnotes moved, and which settings were in force. No timestamp, so a change in it is a change in the conversion rather than in the clock.

## Three things worth your attention

**I could not call it `report.md`.** `fixtures/report.txt` already converts to `report.md`, so a report by that name would silently overwrite the conversion output. I used `<stem>.report.md` (`report.report.md`), which is ugly for that one file. If you'd rather have the literal name, renaming the fixture is the way — say the word and I'll do it.

**I changed one existing behaviour.** The old CLI printed the summary line to stdout even when the Markdown was going there, so `scribe convert x.txt - > x.md` wrote statistics into the document. I moved it to stderr and pinned it with a test. It's a one-line revert if you'd rather keep parity.

**Two things I left alone.** The regexes that recognise headings, bullets, notes and page numbers stay code — the parsers read their capture groups by number, so a mistyped pattern in a config file would fail somewhere far from the typo. And the README's example line said `8 paragraphs` where the code has always produced `12`; I corrected the text, having confirmed against `HEAD` that the count itself didn't change.

One loose end I did not act on: `convert` now drops two untracked files into `fixtures/` instead of one, and the repo has no `.gitignore`. Adding one felt like scope creep, but it's worth a line if these are going to be generated in place.

## What was actually wrong

The threshold was two things, only one of which was a setting:

```python
threshold = max(2, int(len(doc.pages) * REPEAT_SHARE))
```

The hardcoded `2` is a floor — the fewest pages a line must appear on. That's now `min_repeats`. But the floor wasn't what caught your document: at five pages the share gave `int(5 × 0.6) = 3`, and your header appears on two. So exposing the floor alone would have changed nothing, and the default share had to move too.

## Why 0.4 and not 0.5

I laid the thresholds out before choosing:

| pages | 0.6 (was) | 0.5 | 0.4 (now) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 6 | 3 | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| 40 | 24 | 20 | 16 |

`0.5` catches your report, but only because `int(2.5)` truncates to 2 — a six-page report with the same problem would still slip through and you'd be back here. `0.4` is two pages in five exactly, and holds for six and seven. There's a test pinning each.

**The cost, so it's on the record:** this makes furniture stripping more aggressive on long documents. A line near the page edge repeating on 16 pages of 40 is now furniture where it previously took 24 — and `furniture.py` warns that a genuine heading eaten this way is gone before anything can rescue it. If your corpus has section titles that repeat over long chapters, `repeat_share = 0.6` in `scribe.toml` puts it back; I verified that path restores the old behaviour exactly. The conversion report lists what was dropped, so a heading lost this way is visible rather than silent.

Your three fixtures are byte-identical under the new default — at three and four pages the floor was already the binding constraint, so nothing moved.

A threshold of 1 would make every line near a page edge furniture and empty the document rather than tidy it — worth a guard on a knob I was newly exposing. The check lives on the settings class, so it holds however the settings are built, not just when they come from a file.

## 1. Notes in the report

They're now a numbered list in document order, with an excerpt of each:

```
1. `[^1]` The 2019 report describes the method in full.
2. `[^2]` Provisional flights are excluded from the means in section...
```

The left-hand number is the position in the Markdown's footnote list; the marker is the label the note actually carries. Those look redundant here because your source numbers its notes 1, 2, 3 — but they come apart when a document restarts numbering on each page, and that's exactly when you need to cross-reference by position. There's a test built on two pages whose notes run 2 then 1, asserting the report's order matches the Markdown's rather than being sorted.

The ordering was already correct; what was missing was any guarantee it would stay that way. The notes are now recorded in the same loop that writes the definition lines, so the report can't drift out of step with the document.

Long notes are cut at a word, and past twelve the rest are counted — a twenty-note document still gives a report under 45 lines.

## 2. `keep_hyphen` empty by default

The list of twelve prefixes is gone from the code and lives in the config, starting empty. "well-" and "being" now rejoin as "wellbeing" until you say otherwise:

```toml
[paragraphs]
keep_hyphen = ["well", "self"]     # verified: gives well-being, self-esteem
```

`scribe.toml` still carries the old twelve on a commented line, framed as somewhere to start rather than a recommendation. Since the conversion report lists every word it rejoined, that list is where you'd find the prefixes your corpus actually needs.

None of your three fixtures contain a break on one of those prefixes, so the output didn't move — but **this does change conversions of documents that do**, silently and in the body text. Worth a spot-check on anything already converted with compounds in it.

## One thing to know about the test suite

This reversed a policy the original suite asserted directly — `test_a_real_compound_keeps_its_hyphen` was one of the 54 tests I inherited. I rewrote it to assert the new default and to point at the opt-in test, rather than deleting it. The defaults guard in `test_config.py` now records both changed defaults and the argument for each, so the next person to touch them hits the same friction.

I also fixed a fixture trap in my own new tests: a twenty-page document built from one template made every line a repeat, and the furniture rule stripped the notes off the pages before anything looked for them. The test failed loudly, which is the only reason I caught it — the pages carry distinct wording now.
